$description: The `secret` form control (specs/extensions.md §9.1, §13): one password field whose VALUE goes to the platform's secret store and never to project.json. A descriptor names it with `"ui": { "<field>": { "control": "secret" } }`, and `ui/schema-form.ts` mounts it into the empty host its own document announces for that field. **A surface never renders back the secret it describes, and this document is where that is visible rather than remembered**: the only thing bound to the field's value is `#/state/shown`, a scope path whose whole purpose is to hold nothing. What the field is worth is said in the placeholder instead — the env NAME the store gave it, which is the only half of a secret a screen may carry. `ui/form-controls.ts` decides everything else: whether the host has a secret store at all, what the placeholder says, what a commit is worth and what the field persists.

style.$description: `.secret-field` carried no rule anywhere — it was one of `check-styles.ts`'s ALLOWED_ORPHANS, a class emitted only so a test could find the control — so there is nothing to translate and the wrapper takes no box of its own. The field takes the width of the control host the form drew, which is the flex item; a kit field is inline-flex by default and would otherwise sit at its intrinsic width in a row sized for it.

children.$description: `autocomplete: new-password` because this is a place to PUT a secret rather than to prove one: without it a password manager offers to fill the field with a credential belonging to whatever site the reader last logged in to, and the offer is the manager's own UI drawn over an editor. The value binding is `#/state/shown` and nothing else ever writes to it — see the document description.

onchange.description: The change bubbles out of the field's own input, so what the reader typed is read off the event rather than off the element — and it is read here, handed to the flow, and never written back onto the scope.
